title: The September Decision That Sets Up Your Christmas Cash Flow
linkedin:
Spring stock orders and Christmas rosters are being locked in this month, and none of the revenue they're funding has arrived yet.

That's not a mistake. It's the ordinary mechanics of a seasonal trading peak. A retailer paying a deposit on Christmas stock in September won't sell a unit of it for months. A hospitality venue building its casual roster for December starts paying wages in October. A trades business buying materials now won't invoice the work until November.

None of these decisions are wrong. What catches owners out is that the spend and the revenue get modelled as one annual number instead of a week by week picture, so the gap only becomes visible once it's already open, usually in October or November, by which point the stock is ordered and the roster is locked in.

A business can be tracking a genuinely strong result for the full financial year and still hit a real squeeze in spring, because profit and cash move on different clocks. The businesses that get through it calmly aren't spending less. They've mapped, week by week, exactly where the outflow peaks relative to when the season's cash starts coming back in, and decided in advance how that gap gets covered.

September is the month those decisions get made. It's worth mapping the gap before the purchase order goes out, not after.

Full piece on the ProfitPulse blog.

Spring has arrived, and for retailers, hospitality venues and trades businesses across Brisbane, Queensland, New South Wales and Victoria, this is the month Christmas trading gets funded. Stock orders for the festive season are going out now, often with a deposit or full payment due well before a single item sells. Casual staff are being recruited and rostered for December, which means wage costs start climbing from October. Marketing spend for the seasonal push is usually paid up front too.

None of that is a mistake. It's simply how a seasonal trading peak works, and it happens every year to businesses that are otherwise running well and genuinely profitable. What catches owners out is not the spending itself, it's that the gap between that spend and the revenue it's meant to generate often isn't mapped properly until October or November, by which point the stock is ordered, the roster is locked in, and there's little room left to adjust.

The businesses that get through spring calmly have usually mapped, week by week, exactly where that gap opens and decided in advance how to cover it, whether through supplier terms, a facility, or a buffer set aside in advance.

If your Christmas stock order or roster is about to go out and the funding plan behind it still feels like a guess, now is the time to look at it. Read the full piece on the blog.
